description: Inequalities of age, disability, sexuality and religion in contemporary Britain.
content_html:
Inequality Beyond Class and Gender

The GCSE Sociology specification recognises that inequality is not produced only by class or gender. Age, disability, sexuality and religion are each named as dimensions of social inequality that shape the life chances and power of different groups in the UK. Sociologists study these inequalities using the same tools applied to class and gender: evidence of disadvantage, analysis of the mechanisms that produce it, and perspectives that offer competing explanations. This lesson examines each in turn, giving particular attention to the medical and social models of disability — a binary the specification explicitly requires students to explain.

Key Fact

The specification requires students to distinguish two models of disability: the medical model (disability is the impairment in the individual) and the social model (disability is created by societal barriers). These models lead to fundamentally different conclusions about where the “problem” of disability lies and therefore who is responsible for addressing it.

Age Inequality and Ageism

Ageism is the term sociologists use to describe prejudice or discrimination based on age. Unlike some other protected characteristics, ageism affects people at both ends of the age spectrum — the young and the elderly — in different ways.

Youth inequality: Young people in the UK face specific disadvantages. They are over-represented in unemployment statistics and are less likely to own their own homes than previous generations at the same life stage. Young people below the age of 18 cannot vote and have limited political power. Media representations of young people frequently rely on negative stereotypes — the “feral youth”, the anti-social teenager — which can feed into scapegoating of young people for social problems such as crime and benefit dependency. These representations involve a form of labelling that can have real consequences for how young people are treated by police, employers and schools.

Elderly inequality: Older people face a different pattern of disadvantage. Workers over fifty may be passed over for promotion or made redundant in favour of younger employees, in a process of ageist discrimination that limits their earning power and economic security. Older people on fixed or state pensions are vulnerable to poverty, especially when the cost of living rises. Social isolation is more common among older people, limiting their participation in social life. Under-representation of older people in elected politics means their interests — in areas such as social care funding, pension provision and healthcare — may be under-prioritised relative to working-age adults. Functionalists might argue that different treatment of the elderly reflects the reduced functional contribution of those who have retired from active employment; conflict perspectives argue that ageism serves the interests of employers and the state by pushing older workers out of the labour market at reduced cost.

Disability Inequality: Medical and Social Models

Disability is one of the most debated areas of social inequality because sociologists disagree about what disability fundamentally is. The two dominant frameworks are the medical model of disability and the social model of disability.

Medical model: The medical model locates disability within the individual. A person who uses a wheelchair is “disabled” because their body cannot perform the function of walking. The solution, in this framework, is medical intervention — treatment, rehabilitation or prosthetics — to restore the individual as closely as possible to a “normal” state. The focus is on what is “wrong” with the person. Critics argue this model individualises a social problem, treating disabled people as passive patients who need to be “fixed” rather than as citizens who face structural barriers. Historically the medical model has been used to justify institutionalisation and has reinforced stigma by associating disability with deficit.

Social model: The social model, developed by disabled activists and sociologists from the 1970s onwards, locates disability in society rather than in the individual. A person who uses a wheelchair is “disabled” not by their inability to walk but by the absence of ramps, lifts and accessible buildings. The impairment (the physical condition) is distinguished from the disability (the disadvantage created by social barriers). In this framework, the solution is to remove social barriers — to build accessible environments, challenge discriminatory attitudes, and change employment practices. The social model aligns most closely with the sociological discipline because it treats disability as a form of social construction rather than a fixed biological category. Most sociologists prefer the social model because it is consistent with the broader sociological principle that inequality is produced by social arrangements, not by nature. For example: two people with the same hearing impairment may have very different experiences depending on whether their workplace provides British Sign Language interpreters, captioning technology and flexible communication policies. The impairment is the same; the disability (social exclusion, restricted employment) is variable because it depends on social provision.

In contemporary UK, disabled people face significant inequality in employment, income and social participation. The disability employment gap — the difference in employment rates between disabled and non-disabled people — remains substantial. Disabled people are, on average, paid less and are more likely to be in poverty. The Equality Act 2010 places duties on employers to make “reasonable adjustments” to remove barriers, but campaigners argue enforcement is weak and attitudinal barriers remain significant.

Sexuality Inequality: Homophobia and Heteronormativity

Homophobia refers to prejudice, discrimination and hostility directed at people on the grounds of their sexuality. LGBTQ+ individuals have faced, and in many contexts continue to face, significant inequality. In the UK, same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised in England and Wales in 1967 (and later in Scotland and Northern Ireland). Civil partnerships were introduced in 2004, and same-sex marriage was legalised in England and Wales in 2013. These legal changes mark significant shifts in formal equality.

However, sociologists distinguish formal legal equality from lived experience. Heteronormativity — the cultural assumption that heterosexuality is the default — continues to operate through everyday interactions, institutional culture and media representation, even after legal equality has been achieved. Research consistently shows that LGBTQ+ individuals report higher rates of mental health difficulties, including depression and anxiety, linked to experiences of discrimination, bullying and social exclusion. Hate crimes on grounds of sexual orientation continue to be recorded by UK police. Employment discrimination, while illegal, remains reported in survey evidence.

Sociologists working in the interactionist tradition draw attention to how labelling and stigma operate around sexual orientation. Being labelled as “different” or “deviant” in educational and social settings can have lasting effects on mental health and social participation. Feminist sociologists link homophobia to patriarchal norms — gay men and lesbian women challenge traditional gender roles and the heterosexual family form that patriarchal culture treats as normal, meaning homophobia can be understood partly as a defence of patriarchal norms.

Religious Inequality: Islamophobia and Antisemitism

Religion and belief is a recognised dimension of inequality in the UK. The specification explicitly names Islamophobia and antisemitism as documented forms of religious inequality.

Islamophobia has been documented in employment discrimination studies: applicants with identifiably Muslim names receive fewer interview invitations than identical applications with non-Muslim names. Muslim communities have faced increased experiences of hate crime, particularly following major political events. Negative media stereotyping of Muslims — associating Islam disproportionately with violence or extremism — contributes to a climate that can normalise discrimination. Sociologists applying the concept of discrimination note that religious discrimination intersects with ethnicity: many Muslims in the UK are from South Asian or Middle Eastern backgrounds, meaning Islamophobia often combines religious and ethnic prejudice simultaneously.

Antisemitism has a documented history in Europe and remains present in contemporary UK society. Jewish communities have faced stereotyping — often drawing on longstanding conspiracy theories about wealth and power — and recorded hate crimes. Surveys consistently document that a proportion of the UK population holds antisemitic attitudes. Sociologists are careful to present these patterns as empirical evidence of religious inequality, treating antisemitism as a form of prejudice that must be understood sociologically — that is, in terms of its social and historical construction — rather than as a natural or inevitable feature of intergroup relations.

Religious groups can be subject to stereotyping — the reduction of a complex and diverse community to a simple, negative image. These stereotypes can feed directly into labelling processes: an employer who assumes all members of a religious group hold particular attitudes, or are likely to prioritise religious observance over work duties, is applying a stereotype that constitutes direct discrimination. Scapegoating occurs when structural problems — unemployment, housing shortages, crime — are blamed on religious minority groups rather than on economic or political conditions. Historically, Jewish communities in Europe were scapegoated for economic crises. In contemporary UK, some commentary scapegoats Muslim communities for social cohesion problems. Sociologists analyse these processes as social constructions, not as reflections of actual group characteristics.

Key Fact

Age, disability, sexuality and religion are all protected characteristics under the Equality Act 2010. Sociological analysis goes beyond legal protection to ask why inequality persists despite formal legal equality — the answer lies in structural barriers (the social model of disability), heteronormativity, ageist labour market practices, and documented patterns of religious discrimination operating through stereotyping, labelling and scapegoating.
exam_tip_html: A common error on questions about disability is to use only the medical model without presenting the social model — or to confuse the two. The social model argues that disability is created by society through inaccessible environments and discriminatory attitudes, not by the individual’s impairment. The medical model locates disability in the individual. In a 4-mark Describe on disability models, describe both and give a concrete example of each: medical model — a wheelchair user is disabled by their inability to walk; social model — a wheelchair user is disabled by the absence of ramps and lifts. On a 12-mark Evaluate about the causes of inequality for any group covered in this lesson, always present competing perspectives: a functionalist would note some differential outcomes reflect different functional contributions; a conflict perspective (Marxist, feminist, interactionist) would emphasise structural and social barriers rather than individual characteristics. Close with a supported judgement.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Ageism affects both the young (unemployment, political exclusion, negative stereotyping) and the elderly (labour market discrimination, poverty risk, social isolation). Age inequality is produced through structural processes as well as individual prejudice.
  • The medical model of disability locates the problem in the individual's impairment; the social model locates it in the barriers society creates. Most sociologists prefer the social model because it treats disability as a social construction and focuses solutions on removing barriers rather than fixing individuals.
  • Homophobia and heteronormativity produce inequality for LGBTQ+ individuals even after formal legal equality is achieved. Islamophobia and antisemitism are documented forms of religious inequality in the UK, operating through discrimination, stereotyping and scapegoating processes.

practice_questions.text:
Which model of disability argues that disabled people are disadvantaged primarily by social barriers rather than by their individual impairment?
A) The medical model
B) The interactionist model
C) The social model
D) The functionalist model

practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that homophobia involves prejudice or hostility; 1 mark for specifying that it is directed at people on the grounds of their sexuality, particularly lesbian, gay or bisexual people. Example: 'Homophobia is irrational fear, hatred or prejudice directed at people on the grounds of their sexuality, which can take the form of discrimination, harassment or hate crime against lesbian, gay or bisexual individuals.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe the social model of disability.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that the social model locates disability in society rather than in the individual. 2 marks for a developed description with an example: e.g. 'The social model of disability argues that it is not a person's physical impairment that disables them but the barriers society creates — inaccessible buildings, discriminatory attitudes and the absence of support. A person who uses a wheelchair is not disabled by their inability to walk but by the absence of ramps and lifts in public spaces. The solution, in this model, is to remove social barriers rather than to treat or fix the individual.'

practice_questions.text: Describe how ageism affects elderly people's life chances in the UK.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. Ageism involves prejudice or discrimination on the grounds of age (1 mark). Older workers may be passed over for promotion or made redundant in favour of younger employees, reducing their earning power and economic security (1 mark). Older people on fixed pensions are more vulnerable to poverty, especially when living costs rise (1 mark). Under-representation of older people in elected politics means their interests in areas such as social care and healthcare funding may be under-prioritised (1 mark). Any three points developed with sociological vocabulary earn full marks.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that religious inequality in the UK is mainly the result of individual prejudice rather than structural factors.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: at least two perspectives developed in detail, both sides of the debate, sustained sociological vocabulary, supported judgement. Supporting the individual prejudice view: evidence of individual attitudes (surveys documenting antisemitic or Islamophobic views), individual acts of hate crime. Contrasting: structural and sociological account — employment discrimination studies showing systemic disadvantage for Muslim-named applicants; media stereotyping as a structural process that normalises prejudice; scapegoating as a social mechanism where structural economic problems are blamed on minority groups; labelling processes through which religious minorities are categorised and treated differently. Named processes (stereotyping, labelling, scapegoating, discrimination, Islamophobia, antisemitism) used precisely. Supported judgement.

Secure: Both sides covered, key concepts used, judgement offered.

Developing: Relevant points but mostly one-sided; some vocabulary; assertive conclusion.

Emerging: Basic description of religious inequality; few sociological concepts; little evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that the social model of disability is more useful than the medical model for explaining the inequalities disabled people face.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: full range of relevant arguments. Social model explained in depth — disability as social construction, barriers argument, solution lies in removing social barriers not fixing individuals; aligned with broader sociological principle that inequality is produced by social arrangements. Medical model explained — disability located in individual impairment, medical solution, historical context of institutionalisation and stigma. Arguments for the social model: evidence that the same impairment produces very different outcomes depending on social provision; disability employment gap reflects employer attitudes and inaccessible workplaces not just individual conditions; consistent with conflict perspectives (Marxism, feminism) that identify structural rather than individual causes. Arguments for the medical model's continued relevance: some conditions require medical intervention regardless of social provision; the model has enabled advances in treatment that improve quality of life. At least two sociological perspectives considered (interactionist on labelling and stigma; Marxist on how capitalism creates barriers; feminist on intersection of disability and gender). Supported judgement about the relative utility of each model.

Secure: Both models explained with most arguments; judgement offered; named concepts used.

Developing: Both models described but not fully evaluated; limited perspective application; weak conclusion.

Emerging: One model described; little evaluation; few sociological concepts.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following best describes the medical model of disability?
options: Disability is created by societal barriers such as inaccessible buildings and discriminatory attitudes
Disability is located in the individual's impairment and requires medical intervention to address
Disability is a form of achieved status that can be overcome through personal effort
Disability is a social construction with no basis in physical difference

knowledge_checks.q: The cultural assumption that heterosexuality is the default or normal sexual orientation, which marginalises other sexualities, is called:
The social model of disability argues that disabled people are disadvantaged not by their impairment but by the _____ created by society.
Prejudice, hostility and discrimination directed at Muslims or Islam is called _____.
Match each form of inequality to its named concept:
right: Ageism — prejudice or discrimination based on a person's age
Barriers created by society — inaccessible environments and discriminatory attitudes — rather than individual impairment
Antisemitism — prejudice, hostility and discrimination directed at Jewish people

flashcard_questions.a: Prejudice or discrimination on the grounds of a person's age, affecting both younger and older people.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the medical model of disability?
flashcard_questions.a: The view that disability is a medical or physical impairment in the individual that prevents them from performing normal activities.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the social model of disability?
flashcard_questions.a: The view that disability is created not by individual impairment but by the barriers, attitudes and design failures of society.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one example of the social model of disability in practice.
flashcard_questions.a: A wheelchair user is disabled by the absence of ramps and lifts, not by their inability to walk — remove the barriers, remove the disability.
Irrational fear, hatred or prejudice directed at lesbian, gay or bisexual people.
The assumption that heterosexuality is the default or normal sexual orientation, marginalising other sexualities.
Prejudice, hostility and discrimination directed at Muslims or Islam, including negative stereotyping and hate crimes.
Prejudice, hostility and discrimination directed at Jewish people, often involving negative stereotypes and historical persecution.

flashcard_questions.q: How does scapegoating relate to religious inequality?
flashcard_questions.a: Structural problems such as unemployment are blamed on religious minority groups rather than on economic or political conditions.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do sociologists prefer the social model of disability?
flashcard_questions.a: It treats disability as a social construction and focuses solutions on removing barriers rather than fixing individuals — consistent with sociology's structural approach.

flashcard_questions.q: How does feminist sociology explain homophobia?
flashcard_questions.a: Homophobia can be understood partly as a defence of patriarchal norms, since LGBTQ+ people challenge traditional gender roles and the heterosexual family form.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two ways ageism affects elderly people in the UK.
flashcard_questions.a: Labour market discrimination (being passed over for promotion) and vulnerability to poverty on fixed pensions.

glossary_terms.definition: Prejudice or discrimination on the grounds of a person's age, which can affect both younger and older people.
The view that disability is primarily a medical or physical impairment located in the individual, which prevents them from performing activities considered normal.
The view that disability is created not by individual impairment but by the barriers, attitudes and design failures of society.
Irrational fear, hatred or prejudice directed at lesbian, gay or bisexual people, which can take the form of discrimination, harassment or hate crime.
The cultural assumption that heterosexuality is the default or normal sexual orientation, which marginalises and renders invisible other forms of sexuality.
Prejudice, hostility and discrimination directed at Muslims or Islam, including negative stereotyping, hate crimes and employment discrimination.
Prejudice, hostility and discrimination directed at Jewish people, often involving negative stereotypes and documented in hate crime statistics.
Blaming a particular social group for social problems, often deflecting attention from structural causes of those problems.
